newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS-S.AFRICA'S STANDARD TRIMS 0.25 POINT OFF PRIME.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-S.AFRICA'S STANDARD TRIMS 0.25 POINT OFF PRIME.

text.p: South Africa's Standard Bank Investment Corp Ltd on Wednesday announced a surprise quarter point cut in its prime lending rate to 19.25 percent from 19.50, effective October 1.
The base home loan rate is also being reduced by a similar amount to 19 percent.

Standard -- one of South Africa's big four banks -- said the move reflected the government's decision to scrap the Financial Services Levy (FSL) and replace it with value added tax (VAT) on financial services from next month.

But analysts said it also showed an encouraging return to relative stability in South African markets following this year's plunge in the rand which has forced the authorities to keep rates high to attract foreign capital.

"I don't think they would have done it if we hadn't had the favourable market circumstances of the last few days with short rates falling and the rand quite strong, especially against the crosses," said Dave Mohr, chief economist at life assurer Old Mutual in Cape Town.

The rand this week fell back below the 7.0 pyschological level against sterling and has also held its own against a strong dollar. It last traded at 4.48 against the U.S. currency, more than 10 cents up on its record low set in August.
FSL was first introduced by the South African government in 1991, when banks increased prime by 0.25 percent to recover the cost.

Standard Bank chief executive Mike Vosloo said his bank had now decided to pass on the benefits of the levy's removal to its customers. "We are pleased to be able to alleviate some pressure on our borrowers," he said.
Other banks showed no immediate signs of following suit, holding prime at 19.50 percent, but dealers said the move by Standard was likely to force their hand.
On speculated other banks might see fit to reduce their prime rates by more than 25 basis points, triggering a rate war.
South African prime rates were last reduced on June 25, when Amalgamated Banks of South Africa Ltd took its competitors by surprise, announcing a one percentage point cut to 19.50, effective July 1.
That move followed widespread criticism of commercial banks for unilaterally hiking rates by one point to 20.50 percent on May 17 without any lead from the central Reserve Bank.
The Reserve Bank's key has been unchanged since end-April, when it was raised to 16 percent from 15.
Standard's prime rate cut provided a late incentive for the bond market to extend its gains on Wednesday, helping yields to their best levels in nearly eight weeks.
At the finish, the benchmark R150 was pegged at a 15.09 percent yield -- its best level since July 12 when it closed at 15.10 -- and over 10 basis points off its overnight 15.23 percent finish.
However, bond traders added that the fact the rationale for the easing was a technical change in the tax regime would probably limit further gains.
